text: Back in this course's Notifications chapter, you saw gs dot event queue fire a named event that a Notification could react to. That same event queue has another kind of listener besides Notifications: a Script Action — a server-side script that runs whenever a specific named event fires.

Here's the distinction that actually matters. A Business Rule reacts directly to a database operation on a table — insert, update, delete — the platform fires it automatically the instant that happens. A Script Action is different: it reacts to an event, and an event only exists because someone's code explicitly chose to raise it with gs dot event queue. That's loose coupling — the code that fires the event and the code that reacts to it don't need to know anything about each other.

That loose coupling is the real benefit. You can add a Script Action, remove one, or change what it does, without touching the Business Rule that raises the event. And more than one listener can react to the exact same event independently — a Notification and a Script Action, both triggered by the same gs dot event queue call.

Here's a real Script Action listening for an event named vehicle dot returned. Inside the script, the fired event is available as the event variable, and current carries the record tied to the event. This one reads the checkout record's vehicle reference, looks up that vehicle, and marks its status back to available with a fresh last-returned timestamp.

A Scheduled Script is a completely different animal — it's a type of Scheduled Job, time-driven rather than event-driven, with no trigger at all. This example runs nightly at 2 AM, builds a cutoff date 90 days in the past, queries for incidents closed before that cutoff, and flags each one as archived. Nothing a user did today caused this to run — it just runs, on its own clock.

Event-driven and loosely coupled versus time-driven and trigger-free — two more ways server script runs without anyone sitting at a form. Next up: the Scripted REST Lab, where you'll build a resource and a Script Action together in one real scenario.
